**Meanwhile**

There is a word I have grown fond of, and it is *meanwhile*. It is one of those words that does an enormous amount of work while pretending to do very little — a stagehand in a black turtleneck, moving furniture between scenes. *Meanwhile, across town.* *Meanwhile, the water was rising.* It admits something that most sentences cannot afford to admit: that while this thing is happening, so is everything else.

Because that's the problem with attention. It's a spotlight, and spotlights work by producing darkness. Whatever you're looking at is purchased with everything you aren't. Right now, wherever you are, someone is putting a hand on a stair rail. Someone is discovering that the milk has gone off, tipping the carton back upright with a small private grimace. A woman in a city you'll never visit is deciding, on insufficient evidence, that she should probably call her brother. None of this needs you. That's the astonishing part. The world is not a performance staged for observers; it goes on with the lights off, in rooms with no one in them, at the bottoms of lakes.

I think about the unwitnessed a lot. Ninety-nine point something percent of what has ever happened happened with no one watching, or with only the wrong someone watching, someone distracted, someone who wouldn't remember. Whole weather systems, whole animal lives — the tremendous industry of a beetle crossing a stone in Anatolia in 400 BC, an event as real and detailed as anything in a museum, and gone without residue. There's a temptation to call this sad, and a stronger temptation to call it a comfort, and I suspect both moves are a little dishonest, because they're both attempts to make it *about us* again. Maybe the honest response is just a low whistle.

Here's a small thing. In old books you sometimes find pressed flowers. Somebody, some afternoon, decided that this particular buttercup was worth keeping, and put it at page 212, and closed the book. That afternoon had weather in it. It had a smell. The person had probably eaten something an hour before and had opinions about it. All of that has been reduced, by the immense compression algorithm of time, to a brown translucent smear the shape of a flower. And yet the smear is a *message*, in a way — not a message with content, exactly, but a message that says: someone was here, and they were the kind of creature who saves things.

We are the kind of creature who saves things. This seems to me one of the more interesting facts about people, more interesting than most of the things people say about themselves. Not that we make tools — plenty of animals make tools — but that we make *reminders*. Cairns. Knots in handkerchiefs. Tally marks. The whole vast apparatus of writing, which is at bottom a technology for making the past shout at you. Every library is a shouting match with entropy, and entropy is winning, but slowly, and the slowness is where we live.

I notice I've drifted toward elegy, which is a gravitational well that essays fall into if you don't steer. So let me steer.

*Meanwhile* is not really a mournful word. It's a comic word, structurally. It's the word that punctures self-importance. You're in the middle of your crisis, the great turning point of your life, the sentence you'll be revising in your head for thirty years — and *meanwhile*, a pigeon is walking around on the roof above you with its ridiculous mechanical head-bob, entirely uninvolved. This is the mechanism of most good jokes and nearly all good novels: the abrupt widening of the frame. Tolstoy is a genius of *meanwhile*. So is anyone who has ever made you laugh during an argument by pointing at something outside the window.

And there's a practical consolation buried in it. If everything is happening at once, then the version of events in which you are the protagonist is only one of a great many simultaneous accounts, all equally valid, most of which barely mention you. Your worst moment is, from three streets over, nothing at all. Not nothing in the sense of *not mattering* — it matters enormously, locally, the way heat matters locally — but nothing in the sense of not being load-bearing for the universe. You are permitted to be small. I've always found that more restful than being told I'm significant.

What I actually wanted to write about, before *meanwhile* hijacked things, was thresholds. Doorways. The way you can stand in a doorway and be in neither room, which is why doorways are where people say the things they've been not saying. Coats half on. One hand on the frame. There's a whole genre of human speech that only occurs in doorways and in cars, both of which are places where you don't have to look directly at anyone. Sincerity requires an escape route. It requires the possibility of pretending, afterward, that you were basically already leaving.

Maybe that's related. Maybe a doorway is just a *meanwhile* you can stand in — a small architectural admission that life is not made of rooms but of the passages between them, and that we've been furnishing the wrong parts. All the good conversations happen in kitchens, which are not for sitting in. All the important thoughts arrive on stairs, in showers, in the four minutes before sleep — never at the desk, never in the chair specifically purchased for thinking. The mind seems to require a slight lack of ceremony. It won't perform for you. Turn to face it and it becomes a pigeon on a roof, bobbing, uninvolved.

So: 1000 words, more or less, with no destination. I've enjoyed this more than I expected to. There's something about being handed unstructured time — even something like time — that immediately reveals what you actually want to do with it, which in my case appears to be looking sideways at ordinary words until they get strange.

Meanwhile, the milk is going off. Meanwhile, somebody's calling their brother. The buttercup is still at page 212, doing nothing, meaning something, waiting for no one in particular.

I want to write an essay that feels associative and textured, maybe exploring attention or small moments, weaving together concrete images with ideas, and being honest about what emerges naturally rather than overthinking it.

The "meanwhile" concept appeals to me—that strange simultaneity of the world, how language captures things happening at once, the unwitnessed. I could move between specific images and larger thoughts, let it turn somewhere unexpected. I'm aiming for around a thousand words of real prose with specificity and care.
